title: Test a New Work Tool on a Low-Risk Task
subtitle: Adopt tools deliberately instead of adopting them because they are new.
description: Pick one recurring work problem, try one tool on a noncritical task, compare the old and new workflow, then keep, adjust, or drop it based on what you observe.

lifeOsSource.hack: Treat a new work tool as a small reversible comparison rather than a commitment to change the whole workflow.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Choose one recurring low-risk work task, note how you handle it now, try one new tool on a test or noncritical case, compare the result and friction, and decide whether to repeat, adjust, or stop.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What task did I test, what changed in the workflow, what friction appeared, and is the next step to keep, adjust, or drop the tool?

faq.question: How small should the first test be?
faq.answer: Use a task where mistakes are easy to reverse and where you can compare the old and new workflow without committing the team or production process.
faq.answerHtml: Use a task where mistakes are easy to reverse and where you can compare the old and new workflow without committing the team or production process.

faq.question: What should I compare?
faq.answer: Compare the observable things that matter for this task: steps, time, rework, errors, handoffs, clarity, or friction. Choose only the measures that actually affect the decision.
faq.answerHtml: Compare the observable things that matter for this task: steps, time, rework, errors, handoffs, clarity, or friction. Choose only the measures that actually affect the decision.

faq.question: When should I stop trying the tool?
faq.answer: Stop when the tool creates unacceptable risk, requires access you should not grant, handles data in a way your rules do not permit, or simply does not improve the task enough to justify the added friction.

intro.html: Pick one recurring work problem, try one tool on a noncritical task, compare the old and new workflow, then keep, adjust, or drop it based on what you observe.

sections.title: 1. Pick one recurring problem
sections.html: Choose a narrow work task with visible friction. Describe the current workflow before choosing a tool, so the test is tied to a real problem rather than novelty.

sections.title: 2. Try it in a reversible setting
sections.html: Use a test, draft or other noncritical case. Keep the first run small enough that you can undo it and avoid exposing sensitive data or production work to an unapproved tool.

sections.title: 3. Compare the workflows
sections.html: Look at the few observable measures that matter for the task, such as steps, time, rework, errors or handoffs. Record what became easier and what new friction appeared.

sections.title: 4. Keep, adjust or drop
sections.html: Repeat the tool only when another run is justified by what you observed. Otherwise change the setup or stop. A failed small test is useful if it prevents a larger bad adoption decision.
